1: Let us make that difference concrete. Suppose a customer has one thousand rupees in a wallet and purchases an item costing three hundred rupees. The expected remaining balance is seven hundred. That arithmetic is simple, but the workflow raises more questions. What if the request is submitted twice? What if the payment service accepts it but the browser loses the response? A good testing conversation identifies those risks before the team commits to one implementation. Early testing includes asking useful questions, not just running a finished application.

Here is a small acceptance example you can use in a team discussion. Given an account with a registered email address, when the customer requests a password reset, then a single-use link is sent and the account remains protected. Now add two variations: a link that has expired, and a link that has already been used. Agree on the expected outcomes before coding. Notice how one short example reveals several design decisions. Also consider whether the response could reveal which email addresses have accounts; avoid exposing that information unnecessarily.

Try this classification exercise. A calculation test runs without opening a browser. A customer evaluates whether checkout instructions make sense. A team measures response time under concurrent traffic. These activities investigate different risks, so one cannot replace the others. The calculation test gives precise, fast feedback about a rule. Customer observation explores whether the product supports a real task. Load testing examines behavior under stress. A balanced strategy chooses enough of each for the product's circumstances, rather than treating the number of automated checks as a complete measure of quality.

Before you move on, write a miniature test plan for a login feature. Include one successful login, one invalid-password attempt, one session-expiry check, and one access-control check after logout. For every check, state both the input and the observable outcome. Avoid saying only that login should work; specify what a legitimate user can see and what an unauthenticated person must not see. This exercise turns a general quality goal into a practical conversation. Keep your plan, because later lessons will add techniques, artifacts and automation to the same reasoning.
2: Start with a comparison that will remain useful throughout the course. Imagine a team building a customer portal while also receiving production support requests. Its planned feature work benefits from a clear short-term goal, but incoming incidents do not respect a sprint calendar. No single label solves both problems. The team must decide how to plan, how to visualize active work, and how to build reliable software. Scrum provides a framework for product work; Kanban helps manage flow; XP contributes engineering practices; Lean encourages attention to value and waste. Evaluate the problem before selecting the vocabulary.

Walk through a Scrum example. The Sprint Goal is to let new customers register safely. The team selects registration and email verification because they support that goal. A tester asks whether duplicate email addresses are allowed and what happens if a confirmation message arrives late. Developers and testers discuss these examples while work is still small. During the sprint they inspect progress and adapt their plan. If registration passes its happy path but bypasses verification, the team has not established the intended outcome. Finishing tasks is useful only when the increment meets the agreed quality conditions and supports the goal.

Now move the same work onto a Kanban board. Three registration fixes are already in Testing, and the team's illustrative testing limit is three. A developer has finished a fourth change. Simply pushing it into Testing hides the capacity problem. Instead, the team investigates why existing work has not finished. Perhaps accounts cannot receive verification messages in the test environment. Helping restore that environment may finish more valuable work than starting another feature. Work-in-progress limits are a signal to collaborate. They do not mean that an overloaded person must work faster, and they are not a substitute for understanding the system.

Consider XP through a concrete calculation. The portal grants a ten-percent introductory discount on an eligible purchase of one thousand rupees. Write a test expecting a discount of one hundred. Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason. Implement the smallest change that makes it pass. Then improve the code while the check stays green. Add an ineligible-customer case expecting zero discount. This creates a feedback loop in which examples guide the design. Refactoring matters: repeatedly adding special cases without improving the design can produce brittle code even when individual tests pass.

Lean invites a different question: where does the customer wait without receiving additional value? Suppose every small change waits two days for a shared testing environment. Buying another reporting tool might not reduce that delay. The team could provide reproducible environments, isolate test data, or run a smaller set of checks earlier. Before changing the process, record the current delay and its cause. After the experiment, compare the results. Reducing waste does not mean removing evidence needed to judge quality. It means avoiding work and waiting that do not help deliver a useful, dependable outcome.

Here is a selection exercise with three fictional teams. Team A builds a new portal and needs frequent stakeholder feedback around a product goal. Scrum could help structure that inspection. Team B maintains several systems and receives unpredictable requests. Kanban could help expose queues and manage capacity. Team C changes financial calculations frequently. XP practices such as test-driven development and continuous integration could strengthen technical feedback. These are starting hypotheses, not universal prescriptions. Each team should inspect its constraints, run a small process experiment, and decide whether actual customer outcomes and feedback speed improve.

Combining approaches requires clear policies. A Scrum team might visualize work with a Kanban board and limit the number of stories actively being developed. It might also use pair programming for risky calculations and run unit tests on every commit. None of those practices removes Scrum's accountabilities or events. Problems arise when a team adopts labels while dropping the useful feedback loops behind them. Write down how new work enters, when testing begins, what Done means, and how urgent incidents affect planned work. Those agreements are more actionable than saying the team is simply hybrid.

For your practice task, imagine that ten support requests arrive while a portal team is implementing a planned registration improvement. Identify the most urgent customer risk, then describe how you would make the incoming work visible. Decide which active item you would finish before starting another. Finally, choose one engineering practice that could prevent the same defect returning. A strong answer connects the delivery process to a testing action and an observable result. For example, address a production access problem, add a focused regression check, and review whether interruption policies preserved visibility into the remaining feature work.
3: Follow a fictional tester named Asha through a bank-transfer story. The product request says that a customer can transfer money to a saved beneficiary. Before creating test cases, Asha asks what a successful transfer means. Should the recipient see funds immediately? Can a transfer be cancelled? What happens when the source account is frozen? These questions reveal risks that a short user story cannot express alone. The tester contributes by helping the team make its assumptions visible. This work is most useful before an implementation turns an unanswered question into accidental behavior.

Build an example table for a transfer limit of ten thousand rupees. A transfer of one rupee is a small valid example if the agreed minimum allows it. Ten thousand is the maximum valid example. Ten thousand and one should be rejected if the limit is inclusive. Zero, a negative amount and an amount greater than the balance require explicit outcomes. The product team must agree on these rules; a tester should not invent banking policy. Once the rules are confirmed, the table guides focused tests and gives developers concrete examples to discuss.

During development, Asha can inspect a fictional transfer API before the user interface exists. The request includes the source account, beneficiary, amount and a unique request identifier. A successful status code is only one piece of evidence. She also checks the response content, the source balance, the recipient record and any transaction entry. A response that says success while the balance remains wrong is still a failure. When data is sensitive, use synthetic accounts and sanitized evidence. The goal is to verify the business outcome across the relevant components, not merely to collect green HTTP responses.

Explore a timeout carefully. Asha sends a transfer, the network response disappears, and the user selects Retry. There are at least two possible realities: the first transfer failed before processing, or it succeeded but the response was lost. Treating both as a new transaction can debit the account twice. The team should define safe retry behavior, often using an idempotency mechanism. The tester then checks repeated submissions, delayed responses and recovery. This is an example of investigation leading to a design conversation. Reporting only that the spinner remained visible would miss the higher-impact financial risk.

Write a useful blocker update. Instead of saying that testing is blocked, Asha explains that transfer-failure scenarios cannot run because the sandbox cannot simulate service timeouts. She identifies the affected checks, the risk they leave unexamined and the help needed. Meanwhile she can review acceptance examples, validate other API behavior or prepare data. This communicates progress without implying that untested behavior is safe. A clear update helps the whole team make a decision: restore the environment, use a controlled substitute, reduce scope, or explicitly carry an unresolved risk.

Technical knowledge makes investigation more independent. SQL can help compare a transaction record with the displayed balance, provided the tester has appropriate access and understands the schema. Browser developer tools can reveal requests and responses. Version control helps connect a failure with a code change. Automation can repeat a reliable transfer check across builds. But each tool answers only part of the question. A query against one table cannot prove that the complete customer journey is correct, just as a successful click cannot prove that the ledger is consistent.

Consider two testers with different visible results. One reports twenty minor defects after development has finished. Another helps prevent a duplicate-transfer defect during refinement and reports fewer bugs. A simple bug-count ranking could reward the less valuable outcome. Discuss feedback speed, important risks investigated, escaped failures and the reliability of existing checks instead. These measures still need interpretation. A low defect count could reflect prevention, limited testing, or low complexity. The tester's responsibility includes explaining the evidence and its limits so that stakeholders do not mistake a convenient number for an assurance of quality.

Your exercise is to prepare a short handover for the transfer feature. State three agreed business rules, two checks already completed and one unresolved risk. Include a reproducible failure example using fictional account data. Explain who can help resolve the risk and what evidence would support closing it. A strong response might mention inclusive limits, ownership validation, a successful transfer, a rejected insufficient-balance request and an untested timeout recovery path. Notice how this combines analysis, execution and communication. That combination is the practical role of a tester in an Agile team.
4: Imagine that stakeholders ask whether a customer-management release is ready. A dashboard says seventy percent of tests have passed. That number alone cannot answer the question. We need to know which features were tested, which risks remain and whether important failures are unresolved. In this lesson, treat tracking as a way to support a decision. Every chart should have a meaning and a next action. Our fictional release contains registration, profile editing and customer search. We will connect each feature to scenarios, results, defects and a concise release update.

Begin with registration. The team agrees that a valid new address creates an account, a duplicate address is handled safely, and an invalid address cannot complete registration. List the environment, build identifier and account data needed for each check. If outbound email is unavailable, mark email-confirmation scenarios as blocked rather than failed or passed. This distinction matters because a failure indicates observed incorrect behavior, while a blocked result indicates missing evidence. Planning dependencies early makes the dashboard easier to interpret later and gives the team time to restore missing capabilities.

Calculate the illustrative status carefully. There are forty tests: twenty-eight passed, six failed, four blocked and two not run. Twenty-eight out of forty is seventy percent passed across the planned set. Twenty-eight out of thirty-four executed tests is approximately eighty-two percent. Both calculations can be mathematically correct but answer different questions. Label the denominator. More importantly, inspect the six failures: a broken account-ownership check may prevent release even if many visual checks pass. Do not compress blocked work, unexecuted work and failed behavior into a single reassuring percentage.

Write a defect that a colleague can reproduce. Use a title such as Duplicate registration returns an internal error on build forty-two. Specify the test environment, a synthetic existing address, the exact registration action, the expected safe response and the actual error. Attach sanitized evidence and link the relevant story. Severity describes the impact of the defect; priority expresses how urgently the team chooses to address it. They often influence each other but are not interchangeable. A small-looking visual issue might still be urgent before a time-sensitive demonstration, while its functional severity remains low.

Build a balanced dashboard. Show unresolved critical risks, blocked work, test execution and defect trends with enough context to explain changes. If execution falls because the test environment was unavailable, annotate that cause. If the pass rate improves because failing tests were removed, the apparent improvement is misleading unless the scope change is visible. For automation, track unstable checks separately so repeated reruns do not disguise unreliable feedback. Metrics are prompts for investigation. Choose a small set that helps the team decide what to fix, finish or investigate next.

Turn the dashboard into a useful update. Registration and profile editing have been checked on the release candidate. Customer search remains partly blocked by incomplete test data. One critical authorization defect is open. The release decision needs either a verified fix or a clear scope change that removes the exposure. This message is stronger than listing how many tickets moved today. It connects completed work with remaining uncertainty. Include an owner and next step for the blocker so stakeholders understand how the uncertainty can be reduced rather than simply being informed that it exists.

Follow one story through its evidence. Start with the acceptance criteria. Link a set of checks, record their results against the build, create a linked defect for a failure and attach retest evidence after the fix. Then run any relevant regression checks before marking the work complete. These links let another team member reconstruct why the story was judged ready. The exact screens depend on the tracking product; the relationship among requirement, test, defect and evidence matters more than the tool. Avoid duplicating the same status manually in several places where it can drift.

For your practice task, write a release update in four sentences. Say what was tested, what remains, which risk matters most and what help is needed. Use the forty-test example, but do not rely on the pass rate as your recommendation. A good answer could say that most registration scenarios pass, search data blocks four checks, a failed account-isolation scenario is critical, and the team needs a fix plus focused retesting. Now ask whether the release would become acceptable if five cosmetic failures were resolved while the authorization failure remained. The risk-based answer is still no.
5: Use a subscription service as a running example. Customers can start a paid plan, renew it and cancel future renewals. A defect in a color choice is inconvenient; a defect that charges a cancelled account can damage trust and require financial correction. Agile Testing principles help the team choose what to clarify and investigate first. They do not guarantee a defect-free product. Their practical value comes from repeated conversations, focused examples and fast feedback. We will connect each principle to a concrete action on the subscription journey rather than leaving it as a slogan.

During refinement, ask when a cancellation becomes effective. Does access continue until the paid period ends? What happens if cancellation arrives while renewal is processing? Write two examples with timestamps and expected billing outcomes. During implementation, developers can check the billing rule at a low level. During integration, the team checks notifications, payment-provider messages and account access. Before release, regression checks cover existing subscribers. The same rule receives attention at several points because different kinds of evidence become available at different times. Continuous quality is this repeated investigation across delivery.

Shared responsibility becomes visible when a renewal fails. The tester notices an incorrect charge. A developer examines the state transition. The Product Owner clarifies the cancellation rule. Operations helps locate a delayed provider message. A security specialist may check that only authorized people can change subscriptions. Collaboration does not mean everyone has identical skills or that nobody owns a task. It means the team uses its combined expertise to solve the customer problem. A handoff that says testing will handle quality at the end delays that shared understanding until changes are harder to make.

Suppose the business changes from immediate cancellation to access through the end of the paid period. Updating only the user interface leaves several risks. Review acceptance examples, billing logic, account permissions, scheduled renewal jobs and customer messages. Existing automated checks may now encode an obsolete rule. A failing test could indicate either a defect or an intentionally changed expectation; investigate before deleting it. Adaptability means keeping the explanation and the evidence aligned with the current agreement. Fast feedback is useful when it points to a meaningful difference, not when it merely produces a quick red result.

Make risk prioritization concrete. Consider three features: a new theme color, cancellation handling and administrator access. Discuss both how a failure might occur and what its consequences would be. A cancellation defect may lead to unwanted charges; an access-control defect may expose customer information. Those consequences justify deeper scenarios than a minor styling change. A simple risk matrix can support the conversation, but numerical scores are estimates rather than precise predictions. Review the ranking when new information appears. Testing effort should respond to the product's actual exposure, not stay fixed because an early spreadsheet assigned a number.

Maintainable automation starts with clear intent. A browser test should identify the Cancel subscription button through a stable, meaningful locator, arrange its own synthetic customer and verify the resulting subscription state. A screen-coordinate click can break when the layout changes, even if the behavior remains correct. A test that relies on another test to create its account can fail for unrelated reasons. Keep setup independent and assertions connected to customer outcomes. When a check becomes flaky, investigate its data, synchronization and dependencies instead of teaching the team to ignore failures through repeated reruns.

Continuous improvement needs an experiment, an owner and a way to inspect results. If testing begins late every sprint, the team might split one large subscription story into smaller slices and clarify its examples before implementation. Observe whether those slices reach verification earlier and whether important misunderstandings decrease. Avoid changing five unrelated process rules at once, because it becomes difficult to learn which change helped. At the next retrospective, inspect what happened and adjust. Improvement is not the number of action items written on a board; it is a useful change that the team actually tries and evaluates.

Your exercise is to plan testing for a cancellation-rule change. Identify a business example, a technical check, a customer-facing observation and one regression risk. For instance, verify that a cancelled subscription keeps access until the agreed end date, prevents a later renewal and displays an accurate confirmation. Also investigate a delayed payment notification near the cancellation time. Explain which specialists should join the conversation. Finish by choosing one small process improvement that would make future billing changes easier to verify. This links continuous testing, shared responsibility, adaptation, risk awareness and improvement in one practical plan.
6: Start with a delivery rule: orders above a defined qualifying amount receive free shipping. A developer can test the calculation, a product specialist can clarify what counts toward the amount, a customer can explore whether the message is understandable, and an engineer can measure checkout under load. These are complementary views of quality. The quadrants organize the questions so a team notices gaps. They do not prescribe a testing order or assign exclusive ownership to particular job titles. Use the model as a conversation aid and adapt the examples to the risks of the feature you are building.

For quadrant one, isolate a shipping calculation. Suppose the agreed rule gives free delivery when the discounted subtotal is at least one thousand rupees. A low-level test checks nine hundred and ninety-nine, one thousand and one thousand and one. Each test runs without opening a browser or contacting a real payment service. When one fails, the feedback points closely to the calculation. Such tests support development by making small changes easier to evaluate. They still cannot tell us whether the team chose the correct threshold or whether the customer understands the final total.

Quadrant two makes the business rule explicit. Ask whether taxes, gift cards and discount reductions affect eligibility. Use a concrete example: a basket worth eleven hundred receives a two-hundred-rupee discount, leaving a qualifying subtotal of nine hundred. Under our fictional rule, free shipping does not apply. Product, development and testing participants should agree on that result before implementation. The example can become an acceptance check, but the conversation is valuable even before automation exists. An executable scenario with an ambiguous expected result will simply automate an unresolved business question.

In quadrant three, explore the actual customer journey. Add items until shipping becomes free, then apply a coupon that lowers the subtotal below the threshold. Does the page explain why shipping reappeared? Does the total update consistently? Try keyboard navigation and a smaller display. You might find that every calculation is correct while the message leaves people confused. Record the situation, the user's difficulty and the effect on completing checkout. Exploration critiques the product by following observations and questions that a predefined rule check may never have considered.

Quadrant four examines technical qualities. A promotion may send many shoppers through the same calculation and checkout services at once. Define a realistic load model and an agreed response-time target before judging the result. Investigate errors, resource use and recovery as well as average response time. Security testing might check that one customer cannot modify another customer's basket. Reliability testing might simulate a temporary dependency failure. These activities require appropriate environments and authorization. A single passing scan or load run is evidence about the tested conditions, not proof that every technical risk is eliminated.

Map a payment feature across all four views. Quadrant one checks fee and total calculations. Quadrant two uses examples of successful, declined and refundable payments. Quadrant three explores interrupted journeys, confusing messages and unexpected navigation. Quadrant four examines concurrent requests, access control and resilience. Some checks can reasonably fit more than one discussion because intent matters. Do not spend a meeting arguing about the perfect quadrant label while a duplicate-charge risk remains untested. The model succeeds when it helps the team ask a missing question and choose an effective way to investigate it.

Avoid treating the matrix as four equal budgets. A simple internal tool and a public payment platform face different risks. One feature may need extensive security investigation; another may need more usability exploration. Automation also crosses the model. Unit tests are commonly automated, acceptance checks may be automated, and performance tools can automate technical experiments. Human judgment remains necessary when deciding what the results mean and what to investigate next. Describe the risk, select an appropriate activity and identify the evidence you want. Then use the quadrant model to check whether an important perspective has been missed.

For your practice task, take a password-reset feature and propose one activity for each quadrant. A possible low-level check verifies token-expiry calculations. A business example specifies what happens when an expired link is opened. Exploratory testing investigates whether recovery messages are understandable and accessible. Technical investigation examines unauthorized token reuse and behavior under a controlled request spike. Explain why each activity exists, rather than only naming a category. Finish by answering the lesson question: response times during a traffic spike belong naturally in the technology-facing critique represented by quadrant four.
7: Picture an appointment platform with one available time slot and two customers trying to reserve it. The business goal sounds simple, but a screenshot of a successful booking cannot establish that double booking is prevented. Scrum gives the team regular opportunities to clarify, implement and inspect the outcome. It does not place testing in a separate final phase. Throughout this example, distinguish the framework's accountabilities from the specialist skills people bring. A team member can contribute deep testing knowledge while sharing responsibility for creating a usable increment that meets the Definition of Done.

The Product Owner helps maximize product value and manages the Product Backlog. The Scrum Master helps establish Scrum and improve team effectiveness. Developers create the usable increment, and people with testing skills may be part of that group. This use of Developers is broader than programmers alone. A tester is not an external gate that receives all work after everyone else finishes. During a booking discussion, testing expertise can reveal concurrency and cancellation risks while implementation choices are still open. Clear accountabilities help the conversation, but quality still depends on the team's actual collaboration.

Refine the booking story with explicit examples. Given one available slot, when one customer completes a reservation, then the slot becomes unavailable to others. Now ask what happens if two requests arrive almost simultaneously. Only one reservation should succeed under our fictional rule. Add a cancelled reservation and an expired temporary hold. These questions help the team identify work needed to achieve the Sprint Goal. Refinement is an ongoing activity, not a prescribed Scrum event. During Sprint Planning, the team considers the effort to implement and verify the selected work rather than treating testing capacity as an afterthought.

During the sprint, check the availability API while the booking interface is still being built. Send two controlled reservation requests for the same synthetic slot and inspect the stored outcome. Later, connect the interface and verify that the losing customer receives a clear message instead of an unexplained error. Run relevant regression checks after fixes. This sequence obtains different evidence as components become available. A timeline that assigns development to the first week and all testing to the last days can hide unresolved work until the sprint is nearly over.

The Definition of Done provides a shared quality baseline for the increment. A team might require reviewed code, passing relevant automated checks, completed security conditions and updated operational information where needed. Acceptance criteria describe expectations for a particular backlog item; the Definition of Done describes quality conditions for the increment. They are related but serve different purposes. If required verification has not happened, calling the work Done misrepresents its state. Make the gap visible and adapt the plan. Pressure to improve a completion chart should not change the meaning of the shared agreement.

At the Sprint Review, stakeholders inspect the booking outcome and discuss what to do next. Perhaps users need a clearer explanation when their chosen slot disappears. That feedback can influence the Product Backlog. The Retrospective looks at how the team worked and how to become more effective. If concurrency testing started late because the environment lacked suitable data, the team might automate creation of isolated slots. These conversations have different purposes. A demonstration alone is not the whole Sprint Review, and a list of complaints without a practical improvement experiment does not make a useful Retrospective.

Use a ten-working-day sprint as an illustration, not a mandatory calendar. On the first days, the team can clarify examples while beginning small implementation slices. As APIs emerge, focused checks and code reviews provide feedback. Integrated journeys, exploration and regression continue as the increment grows. The Daily Scrum helps Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan. It is not simply a status report to a manager. The exact daily distribution changes with the work. What matters is maintaining transparency and finishing usable slices instead of accumulating a late queue of unverified features.

Your exercise is to assess a booking story at the end of a sprint. The main reservation journey works, but the required simultaneous-request check has not run. The team has no evidence that double booking is prevented. If that check is part of the agreed quality conditions, the work is not Done. Explain the missing evidence, investigate whether the scope can be adapted and avoid presenting uncertainty as success. Then propose one improvement for the next sprint, such as preparing concurrency data earlier. This connects honest inspection with a concrete way to improve delivery.
8: Begin with a checkout rule: an eligible member receives a ten-percent discount, but an expired coupon must be rejected. There are several questions hidden inside that sentence. We need to clarify eligibility, calculate the amount, investigate limits and observe the user journey. TDD, BDD, ATDD and exploratory testing can help, but they work at different points and with different intentions. Test design techniques help choose examples systematically. The objective is not to use every method on every story. It is to choose methods that give useful evidence about the most important risks.

For a TDD demonstration, write a small test saying that a purchase of one thousand rupees produces a one-hundred-rupee discount for an eligible member. Confirm the test fails because the function has not implemented that behavior. Add the smallest implementation that makes it pass. Refactor the design while keeping the test green. Next, add an ineligible-customer case expecting zero. These examples should guide the code in small steps. Writing all production code first and adding tests afterward can still be useful, but it does not provide the same design feedback loop as test-driven development.

For BDD, gather product, development and testing perspectives before choosing automation syntax. Ask how a customer knows that a coupon was accepted and how the final total should change. Express an example: given an eligible member with a qualifying basket, when a valid coupon is applied, then the agreed discount appears and the total is updated. Now discuss an expired coupon and a basket below the minimum. Given, When and Then can make examples readable, but the format is not the purpose. The purpose is a shared understanding of observable behavior, including situations where assumptions differ.

ATDD also brings acceptance examples forward. For a refund feature, agree that an eligible cancelled purchase returns the correct amount and changes the order state. Include an ineligible refund, a partial refund and a delayed provider confirmation if those apply to the product. The team can use these examples to guide implementation and later verification. BDD and ATDD overlap in collaborative discovery and examples; their labels do not define a rigid boundary for every team. What matters is that acceptance expectations are clear before code is judged complete, and that the checks reflect real business outcomes.

Exploratory testing adds responsive investigation. Set a charter: investigate whether coupon changes can leave checkout totals inconsistent. Begin with a normal purchase, change quantity, apply a coupon, navigate backward and return. Observe what changes and follow surprising behavior. Record the data, actions and findings so another person can understand the investigation. A timebox helps focus the session, but curiosity should still respond to evidence. Exploration is not random clicking. It combines learning, test design and execution while the tester updates the next question based on what the product actually does.

Use equivalence partitioning and boundaries for a coupon that accepts whole-number quantities from one through ten. Valid quantities form one partition; zero and negative values are invalid; values above ten are invalid. Representative examples can reduce redundant checks. Boundary analysis gives special attention to zero, one, ten and eleven. Other values may be needed depending on the input type and risks. If the input permits decimals or text, those introduce additional partitions. The specification must define the expected result. A technique helps choose inputs, but it cannot resolve an unclear rule about whether a particular input is allowed.

Build a decision table for two conditions: the customer is a member, and the coupon is valid. There are four combinations. Agree on the outcome for a member with a valid coupon, a member with an invalid coupon, a nonmember with a valid coupon and a nonmember with an invalid coupon. Maybe membership is required, or maybe the coupon is available to anyone; the product rule decides. A table makes missing combinations visible. Add columns only when they affect the decision, because many independent conditions can produce more combinations than a team can practically test through the interface.

For your exercise, design checks for a discount feature with a minimum spend of five hundred rupees. State whether the threshold is inclusive, then choose values immediately below, at and above it. Add an expired coupon example and one combination of membership and eligibility. Finally, write a short exploratory charter about changing the basket after applying a coupon. Explain which method supports each part. Boundary analysis addresses the threshold, shared examples clarify behavior, and exploration investigates interactions. The strongest plan combines these views while avoiding multiple expensive checks that all prove the same narrow rule.
9: Imagine joining a team just before release. The invoice feature looks finished, but nobody can explain which account-isolation checks ran or which build contains the last fix. More documents would not automatically solve the problem. Useful artifacts would connect the customer need, expected behavior and evidence. Agile values working software, while still recognizing that documentation can support collaboration and decisions. In this lesson we create a small, connected set of artifacts for a monthly invoice download. Every artifact should answer a practical question for someone who needs to understand, verify, operate or change the product.

Write the user story in terms of the customer goal: a customer wants to download a monthly invoice to keep a record of charges. Then clarify the acceptance criteria. Only completed billing periods are available, the output is a readable PDF, and customers can access only their own invoices. Add an example of a month with no charge if the business needs it. Criteria should describe observable outcomes rather than merely repeat interface labels. A story that says there is a Download button is incomplete if it never explains which document the button must retrieve or who is allowed to retrieve it.

Create one test case with enough detail for its risk. Its identifier is INV zero one. The precondition is a synthetic customer with a completed billing period and a known invoice. The action is to request that period's download. The expected result is the correct PDF with the agreed account and charge information. Record the environment and build when executing it. A second test should investigate access to another synthetic customer's invoice. Detailed steps are useful where precision matters, but a simple low-risk visual check may only need a checklist. Match the detail to the reader's need and the consequences of ambiguity.

Suppose modifying the invoice identifier returns another account's document. Write a defect that explains the authorization failure without exposing real customer information. Include the environment, synthetic account relationship, reproduction steps and observed result. State the expected denial and attach sanitized evidence. Link the affected requirement and test. Avoid putting access tokens or confidential invoices in a broadly shared ticket. The report should help the team reproduce and prioritize the problem, not create a second exposure. After the fix, retain enough retest evidence to show which build was checked and what outcome was observed.

A one-page strategy can describe scope, important risks, environments, responsibilities and the mix of automated and human checks. For this feature, highlight account isolation, document accuracy and availability. Add an exploratory charter: investigate invoice access across roles and billing periods using synthetic accounts. A charter sets a mission while leaving room to follow discoveries. After the session, capture what was covered, what was found and what remains uncertain. This is more useful than a long plan copied from an unrelated project that nobody updates or uses when making a release decision.

Traceability can be lightweight. Connect the account-ownership rule to the unauthorized-download check. Link the failing result to the defect, then the fix and retest. Someone reviewing release readiness can follow that chain and understand why the risk is considered addressed. The same principle applies to automated results: retain the build and relevant report rather than only a screenshot of a green badge. Avoid maintaining multiple disconnected copies of the same relationship in spreadsheets and tickets. A small set of current links is easier to trust than a large matrix that stopped reflecting the product several sprints ago.

Decide what to keep current. Stories and criteria describe the agreed behavior. Important tests preserve repeatable checks. Defect reports record actionable failures. Automated reports show what ran on a build. Operational notes explain relevant deployment or support concerns. Release notes communicate changes to their intended audience. Each artifact has a different reader and lifespan. When behavior changes, identify which artifacts now contain an obsolete rule. Documentation debt grows when old expectations remain easy to find but hard to distinguish from current guidance. Prefer concise material with clear ownership and a visible relationship to the implementation.

For your exercise, create a miniature evidence chain for the invoice authorization defect. Write one criterion, one negative test, a concise defect title and a retest note. The criterion restricts downloads to the owning customer. The test attempts access from a different synthetic account. The defect states that the file was returned. The retest note identifies the fixed build and the observed denial. Explain why a screenshot alone would be insufficient if it omitted the account context and build. Useful documentation allows another person to reconstruct the decision without needing the original tester to explain every missing detail.
10: Picture a support team receiving authentication failures, dashboard requests and small mobile fixes throughout the day. Work arrives continuously, so the team needs visibility into what is active, what is waiting and what is becoming old. Kanban helps the team define and improve that flow. A board is part of the approach, but the board alone cannot solve capacity problems. The team also needs explicit policies, limits and regular inspection. We will follow five fictional requests and show how testing contributes to finishing valuable work rather than becoming an invisible queue near the end.

Define the workflow before drawing columns. Backlog contains possible work, Ready contains requests that meet the team's entry policy, Development contains active implementation, Testing contains active or queued verification, and Done meets the agreed completion policy. These are illustrative choices, not required Kanban column names. Make the start and finish points explicit because metrics depend on them. A blocked item should remain visible in the system with its blocker, rather than being moved somewhere that hides its age. The board should represent how work actually flows, including waiting that the team may otherwise overlook.

Suppose Testing has a limit of three items and already contains three. Two depend on an unavailable environment, while the third needs a small fix. Starting several more features increases active work without increasing finished value. The team might help restore the environment and pair on the small fix. When an item finishes, capacity becomes available to pull more. A limit is a policy that encourages this discussion; it is not a magic number copied from another team. Review whether the chosen limits support collaboration and manageable flow, then adjust through explicit experiments rather than quietly ignoring them.

Use timestamps to explain flow measures. A request arrives Monday, becomes active Wednesday and finishes Friday. If the team measures request-to-finish time, that includes the waiting before Wednesday. If its cycle-time boundary starts when work becomes active, the earlier waiting is outside that measure. State whether you use elapsed calendar time or working time. The current Kanban Guide emphasizes work in progress, throughput, work item age and cycle time as flow metrics. Lead time is also used in practice, with boundaries that must be defined. Unlabelled numbers from different workflows should not be compared as though they describe the same thing.

A constantly full Testing column is a signal, not a diagnosis. The cause could be unstable environments, large batches, missing acceptance criteria, poor testability or a capacity mismatch. Examine individual items and their waiting time before proposing a solution. If every item waits for the same shared account, creating isolated data may help more than adding another dashboard. If large changes arrive in batches, smaller slices and earlier checks may reduce the queue. The objective is better flow through the whole system, so moving a bottleneck to another column without improving completion does not establish success.

Classes of service make tradeoffs explicit when the team chooses to use them. A production authentication outage may qualify for expedited handling under an agreed policy. A normal dashboard enhancement follows standard capacity. A contractual deadline may require a fixed-date policy. These are complementary practices, not mandatory labels for every Kanban system. Too many expedited items undermine predictability because ordinary work is repeatedly interrupted. Define who can invoke an urgent policy, what evidence is needed and how interrupted work remains visible. Priority should reflect consequences and commitments rather than whoever asks most loudly.

Walk through the five requests. One is an active production login failure, two are routine dashboard improvements, one is a mobile display defect and one is a reporting change with a future commitment. Assess the login incident first because customers cannot access the service. Apply the agreed urgent policy and make the interruption visible. Keep the other items ordered according to value, risk and capacity. After the incident fix, verify the important login journeys and capture a regression check where useful. Then inspect the cause so that the team learns from the interruption instead of simply celebrating a fast ticket closure.

For your exercise, investigate a Testing queue that has remained full for a week. Record each item's age, its blocker and the work needed to finish it. Choose one action that could reduce waiting across several items, such as restoring a shared dependency or preparing independent test accounts. Decide how you will observe whether the action improves completion. Do not assume the busiest-looking column is the only problem; it may reflect issues upstream. A strong Kanban discussion connects visible work, explicit policies and evidence about flow to a practical experiment that the team can inspect.
11: Imagine a team with many testing products but slow feedback and frequent escaped payment defects. More tools would not automatically fix the problem. The team must first identify what evidence it needs and where a tool can produce it reliably. In this lesson, connect tools to activities: tracking helps communicate work, API clients inspect service behavior, browser and mobile frameworks repeat journeys, performance tools explore load and CI coordinates checks. Product interfaces change over time, so focus on the underlying workflow. A good toolchain makes important outcomes easier to investigate and failures easier to understand.

For a login-lockout defect, use an issue tracker to connect the affected story, the observed failure and the verification work. Include the build, synthetic account setup and expected policy. An issue tracker can help make responsibility and status visible, but it does not determine whether the policy is correct. Avoid copying sensitive credentials into a ticket. When the fix is ready, record the retest outcome and relevant regression results. Whether the team uses Jira, Azure DevOps or GitHub Issues, the important relationship is the same: expectation, evidence, defect, fix and verification remain understandable together.

Use an API client to send a fictional login request in a test environment. Check a valid account, an incorrect password, missing required fields and an expired token where the contract defines that behavior. Inspect the status, response body and resulting state. The exact expected status codes must come from the API specification; do not assume every product uses identical codes. A successful response alone does not prove permissions are correct. Follow it with an authorized operation and an operation the account must not perform. Use synthetic secrets and keep environment files with credentials out of shared reports.

A browser check can visit the login page, fill clearly identified controls, submit and verify a meaningful signed-in outcome. Prefer user-facing locators or stable test identifiers over fragile page coordinates. Arrange independent data so one failed test does not break the next. For mobile, choose a framework compatible with the application and required platforms; Appium is one option. Decide which journeys justify the cost of end-to-end execution. Repeating every arithmetic rule through a full browser session makes feedback slower and can introduce unrelated failure points that a focused lower-level check avoids.

For performance work, define a realistic scenario and an agreed target before running a tool such as k6 or JMeter. Track errors and response-time distributions alongside throughput. Averages can hide slow experiences for some requests. Security tools such as OWASP ZAP can identify some classes of web issues in an authorized environment, but a scan is not a complete security assessment. Business-rule abuse and access-control mistakes may require targeted investigation. Tool output is a starting point for interpretation. Confirm important findings and explain the conditions under which a measurement or observation was collected.

A CI pipeline can begin when a commit is pushed. Build the application, run focused unit checks, run integration checks and deploy to an isolated test environment if appropriate. Then execute a smaller set of critical end-to-end journeys. Jenkins and GitHub Actions can orchestrate such stages, while actual capabilities depend on the configured project. When a check fails, retain useful logs and sanitized artifacts. Keep fast feedback close to the change, and avoid making every commit wait for a long experiment that could run at another appropriate point. The pipeline should provide reliable signals rather than merely execute many commands.

Prioritize automation by risk, repeatability and maintenance cost. Stable billing calculations often suit focused unit tests. Service contracts suit API and integration checks. A small number of critical customer journeys suit browser or mobile checks. Human exploration remains valuable for new behavior and unexpected interactions. Review flaky tests because a check that randomly fails can teach people to ignore real failures. A retry may help diagnose instability, but it should not erase the evidence. Assign ownership to important checks and remove obsolete expectations when product behavior intentionally changes.

Your exercise is to design a toolchain for a subscription checkout change. Identify one tracking artifact, one calculation check, one API scenario and one end-to-end journey. Add a controlled performance question if traffic is a material risk. Explain where each check runs and what a failure would tell the team. For example, verify fee arithmetic quickly, verify payment-state transitions at the API layer and verify one complete sandbox purchase through the interface. This plan produces clearer feedback than automating every rule only through the browser, because failures can be investigated closer to the component and risk involved.
12: Our fictional platform lets customers register, find appointments, reserve a slot, pay and receive confirmation. Staff use an administrative dashboard, while a mobile app and website share backend services. A customer sees one journey, but the system contains several boundaries where information can be delayed or misunderstood. We will build a connected testing plan across three illustrative sprints. The schedule is a teaching example, not a requirement that real teams deliver these exact features in separate sprints. Focus on how each increment adds evidence and how earlier checks continue protecting behavior as the product grows.

Refine the journey before implementation. A reservation must belong to the requesting customer, a slot must not be confirmed for two people and a payment outcome must update the booking consistently. Ask when temporary holds expire, how cancellation affects availability and what happens if a notification arrives late. Identify dependencies among identity, availability and payment services. Translate the highest risks into examples that product, development and testing participants can understand. This prevents the team from treating five attractive screens as five independent features when their correctness actually depends on shared state and coordinated outcomes.

In the first sprint, test registration and login with synthetic accounts. Check valid input, rejected input, duplicate addresses, recovery and session behavior. Now send two registration requests for the same address close together. A defect could allow duplicate accounts if the implementation checks availability and creates the record as separate unprotected steps. Record the observed outcome, discuss a safe implementation and retest the fix. Add an appropriate regression check. The important lesson is not a particular database command; it is that a realistic concurrency question can expose a defect that sequential happy-path checks miss.

In the booking increment, create one isolated appointment slot and two customers. Send competing reservation attempts. Under the agreed rule, exactly one should succeed and the stored booking must match the winning customer. Check the response for the unsuccessful customer and confirm that it offers an understandable next step. Cancel the successful reservation if the policy permits it, then verify whether availability returns as agreed. Also explore stale screens: a customer may select a slot that someone else reserved moments earlier. The interface and the backend must work together to handle that change safely.

For payments, stay in the provider's sandbox. Test success, decline, user cancellation, delayed confirmation and a repeated callback. Suppose the provider accepted payment but the platform lost the response. A retry should not create a second charge or second booking. Define the recovery policy and examine how unique request identifiers and payment-state transitions support it. Verify records as well as the displayed message. A page saying Payment failed while the provider recorded success is a serious inconsistency. Capture the evidence and add focused checks for the failure mode rather than relying only on the standard successful purchase journey.

As new increments arrive, rerun relevant checks across identity, booking and payment. A permission change in the dashboard could affect existing customer access. A payment-state fix could accidentally prevent cancellation. Add nonfunctional questions where the risks justify them: concurrent search traffic, keyboard accessibility, account isolation and recovery after a dependency failure. Use realistic synthetic data and record the tested conditions. No single green pipeline proves complete readiness. Combine automated results with exploratory findings, unresolved defects and operational evidence to explain what is known and what uncertainty remains.

Before release, inspect the shared quality conditions, open risks, deployment steps and recovery plan. Make sure relevant evidence belongs to the intended release candidate. If a serious unresolved payment issue remains, either resolve it or make an explicit scope and release decision with the responsible stakeholders. After deployment, monitor error signals, transaction consistency and customer feedback using appropriate access controls. A successful deployment command is not the end of quality work. Production observations can reveal conditions that the test environment did not reproduce, and those observations should inform both fixes and future checks.

Your final exercise is to present a release recommendation for this platform. Name the three highest risks, give one piece of evidence for each and identify any remaining uncertainty. A strong response connects duplicate-registration checks, competing-booking results and payment-recovery verification to specific builds and conditions. It also explains how the team will detect problems after release. Look back at the whole course: principles guided priorities, methods shaped examples, artifacts preserved evidence, tools accelerated feedback and collaboration connected the work. You now have a practical way to discuss Agile Testing as part of delivering a product, from the first question through production learning.
